newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Croatian Serbs warn of exodus from rebel enclave.
newsitem.headline: Croatian Serbs warn of exodus from rebel enclave.

text.p: A Croatian Serb leader warned on Thursday that Zagreb's decision to divide Eastern Slavonia into two counties when it reverts to Croatian rule this summer could lead to a mass exodus from the region.

"The situation in Eastern Slavonia is awful," Serb leader Vojislav Stanimirovic told a news conference in Belgrade, adding that there was fear, dissatisfaction and tension in the region since Zagreb announced its decision.

The enclave, which seceded from Croatia in 1991, when Zagreb sought independence from federal Yugoslavia, is to revert to Croatian rule this summer. The mandate of U.N. mission (UNTAES) in the region ends on July 15.

Croatia last week offered a reconciliatory package of rights to the Serbs, including a two-year exemption from service in the Croatian army and the right to vote in areas where they lived before the war.
The Serbs dismissed it as unsatisfactory, demanding that the enclave remain a single administrative unit and not be divided into two counties as envisaged by the Croatian constitution.
An UNTAES spokesman dismissed Stanimirovic's demands.
"We told them (Serbs) it was not possible. Even before the war, it had never been a single unit," Philip Arnold told Reuters by telephone from the enclave.
"It is wrong for local leaders to excite people with such ideas as they know very well that the only places they can go if they leave are not very nice. They can only be exiles."
Local and regional elections throughout Croatia are scheduled for March 16. Eastern Slavonian Serbs are due to take part in the voting for the first time since their 1991 rebellion.
Stanimirovic said the election date was too early, as no census had been made, no electoral districts established and no political parties formed and registered.
"There is a political goal behind this date -- to force the Serb population to accept Croatian documents and citizenship, as a precondition for taking part in the elections," he said.
Croatia has conditioned the right to vote on possession of proper Croatian citizenship papers and said it would respect the pre-war 1991 census in the voting.
Arnold said 30,000 had been issued Croatian papers so far.

It is still unclear exactly how many of the 120,000 Serbs living in Eastern Slavonia will vote in March. About half of them are Serb refugees who fled Croatian army offensives which recaptured their rebel enclaves in 1995.

Croatian President Franjo Tudjman on Wednesday urged Serbs in the enclave to participate fully in the voting and the national parliament said the rights given to Serbs were wider than those given to any other minority in the country.
"Those who interpret Croatia's package as negative don't intend to stay and live under Croatian rule," Defence Minister Gojko Susak told daily Vjesnik in a Thursday interview.
